name: Margaret Whitlock
presenting_complaint: Transient loss of consciousness (collapse) with rapid recovery

medical_history.social: Lives alone. Holds a current driver's licence and drives daily. Non-smoker.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 68-year-old woman presents after a transient loss of consciousness at home earlier today. She recovered fully within a minute. She takes an antihypertensive and a diuretic, drives daily, and has a family history of sudden death. She is now haemodynamically stable (BP 128/78, HR 74, GCS 15). The task is to separate benign from dangerous syncope.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: The history is the investigation: posture, prodrome, exertion, chest pain, palpitations, duration, witness account
Recovery time, injury, incontinence, tongue biting (seizure vs syncope discrimination)
Red flags: syncope on exertion or while lying down, no warning, palpitations first, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, age over 60
Medication review: antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics
Family history of sudden cardiac death (brother died at 52) documented
objective: 12-lead ECG in EVERYONE — look for long QT, Brugada, delta wave/WPW, heart block, ischaemia, LVH
Lying and standing blood pressure (postural drop)
Cardiovascular exam: murmurs (aortic stenosis, HOCM), signs of heart failure
Neurological exam and injury survey from the fall
Bloods: FBC, UEC, BGL, beta-hCG if relevant; echo, telemetry, Holter as indicated
assessment: Syncope — categorise as cardiac vs neurally-mediated/vasovagal vs orthostatic
Identify red-flag features suggesting cardiac cause (exertional, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECG)
Consider arrhythmia, structural heart disease, and medication-related postural hypotension
plan: State the goal explicitly: separate benign from dangerous syncope (FIRST)
12-lead ECG for every syncope patient; lying and standing BP
Bloods (FBC, UEC, BGL, beta-hCG if indicated); echo, telemetry/Holter as indicated
Admit and monitor on telemetry if red flags present (exertional, abnormal ECG, family history of sudden death, structural heart disease)
Review and rationalise the drug chart (antihypertensives, diuretics contributing to postural drop); falls assessment
Give driving advice per Austroads fitness-to-drive guidelines and document it
Safety-netting: advise return if recurrence, chest pain, palpitations; document follow-up/cardiology referral

critical_errors: Forgetting the driving conversation — failing to give and document Austroads driving advice/restriction
Discharging a patient with red-flag (cardiac) syncope without ECG, telemetry or admission
must_not_miss: 12-lead ECG performed and reviewed for long QT/Brugada/WPW/heart block/ischaemia
Cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, structural) worked up vs neurally-mediated vs orthostatic
Austroads driving advice given and documented; safety-netting recorded
